claims.text: Intermediate-temperature tensile loading enhances atomic diffusion in CrMnFeCoNi.
Stress-enhanced diffusion promotes Cr-, Ni-, and Mn-containing nanoclusters at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary nanoclusters weaken grain-boundary cohesion.
Nanocluster-induced loss of grain-boundary cohesion causes a transition from ductile behavior at room temperature to brittle behavior at intermediate temperature.
The proposed initial material is single-phase CrMnFeCoNi with uniform grain size and no pre-existing elemental clustering.
The controlled comparison uses tensile tests at room temperature and 200–400°C in an inert or vacuum atmosphere.
Atom probe tomography before and after deformation can quantify the proposed grain-boundary elemental nanoclustering.
Atomic diffusion is expected to be enhanced in the proposed 200–400°C test range relative to room temperature.
Applied tensile stress and increased atomic mobility drive rapid migration of Cr, Ni, and Mn to grain boundaries.
The resulting nanoclusters act as local stress concentrators.
Nanocluster-associated stress concentration and cohesion loss cause earlier crack initiation.
Brittleness can emerge while the alloy retains an overall single-phase structure.
Intermediate-temperature testing will produce a higher grain-boundary nanocluster density than room-temperature testing.
Intermediate-temperature testing will reduce ductility and toughness relative to room-temperature testing.
Earlier crack initiation and altered fracture-surface morphology will correlate with the extent of nanoclustering.
Room-temperature tensile deformation of the same alloy is expected to show uniform deformation, minimal grain-boundary nanoclustering, and ductile failure.
The predicted behavior is limited to controlled strain rates and oxidation-free conditions within the proposed temperature range.
Composition, microstructural history, and testing conditions may alter nanoclustering kinetics and the magnitude of toughness degradation.
